name: Sanballat, Geshem, and Noadiah
charge: Mocking, conspiring, and hiring prophecy to frighten the builder off the wall
summary: They laughed the work to scorn, then mocked it, then sent four times to draw Nehemiah down to the plain of Ono, then wrote an open letter accusing him of rebellion, then hired a prophet to make him sin in fear. Nehemiah answered every stage and finished the wall, and left their case with God.
offense: Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mocked the rebuilding and represented it as rebellion. When ridicule did not stop the work, the opposition turned to conspiracy and intimidation. Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invited Nehemiah to Ono, intending mischief; an open letter then accused him of seeking to make himself king (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1-8; 6:1-9). Shemaiah urged Nehemiah to hide within the temple, but Nehemiah perceived that God had not sent him. Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to induce fear and sin, providing grounds for an evil report. Noadiah and other prophets also sought to frighten him (Nehemiah 6:10-14). A claim to prophecy became another instrument in the effort to stop the work.
judgment: Nehemiah refused the trap, denied the invented report, and prayed that God would strengthen his hands and remember the adversaries according to their works. The account names no executed personal sentence against these opponents. It does record the defeat of their purpose. The wall was finished, and the surrounding peoples recognized God's hand in it. Tobiah's correspondence and influence continued, but neither repeated pressure nor a religious disguise had made the accusation true or the work cease.

verses.text: But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?
Then answered I them, and said unto them, The God of heaven, he will prosper us; therefore we his servants will arise and build: but ye have no portion, nor right, nor memorial, in Jerusalem.
But it came to pass, that when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews.

And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?
Now Tobiah the Ammonite was by him, and he said, Even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall.

Now it came to pass, when Sanballat, and Tobiah, and Geshem the Arabian, and the rest of our enemies, heard that I had builded the wall, and that there was no breach left therein; (though at that time I had not set up the doors upon the gates;)
That Sanballat and Geshem sent unto me, saying, Come, let us meet together in some one of the villages in the plain of Ono. But they thought to do me mischief.
And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
Yet they sent unto me four times after this sort; and I answered them after the same manner.
Then sent Sanballat his servant unto me in like manner the fifth time with an open letter in his hand;

Wherein was written, It is reported among the heathen, and Gashmu saith it, that thou and the Jews think to rebel: for which cause thou buildest the wall, that thou mayest be their king, according to these words.

And thou hast also appointed prophets to preach of thee at Jerusalem, saying, There is a king in Judah: and now shall it be reported to the king according to these words. Come now therefore, and let us take counsel together.
Then I sent unto him, saying, There are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart.
For they all made us afraid, saying, Their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done. Now therefore, O God, strengthen my hands.
And, lo, I perceived that God had not sent him; but that he pronounced this prophecy against me: for Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
Therefore was he hired, that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin, and that they might have matter for an evil report, that they might reproach me.
My God, think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear.
So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.

And it came to pass, that when all our enemies heard thereof, and all the heathen that were about us saw these things, they were much cast down in their own eyes: for they perceived that this work was wrought of our God.
But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.
And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the Lord hath not spoken?

When a prophet speaketh in the name of the Lord, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.

entries.commentary: In the month Nisan in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, wine is before him and Nehemiah takes up the wine and gives it to the king. This is Artaxerxes the first, the king that came after Ahasuerus of the book of Esther. Nehemiah had not before been sad in the king's presence, for a cupbearer must be of a cheerful countenance, so the king asks why his countenance is sad seeing he is not sick, saying this is nothing but sorrow of heart, and Nehemiah is very sore afraid.

Nehemiah answers, Let the king live for ever, why should not his countenance be sad when the city, the place of his fathers' sepulchres, lies waste and its gates are consumed with fire. The king asks what request he makes, and Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven before he answers, seeking the Most High even in that moment before the king.

Nehemiah asks that if it please the king and if his servant have found favour, the king would send him to Judah, to the city of his fathers' sepulchres, that he may build it. The king, the queen also sitting by him, asks how long his journey would be and when he would return, so Nehemiah sets him a time, and it pleased the king to send him.

Nehemiah asks for letters to the governors beyond the river to convey him until he comes into Judah, and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king's forest to give him timber for the beams of the gates, the wall, and the house he would enter. The king grants him all this according to the good hand of his God upon him. Nehemiah had already prayed, and the Most High heard him and put it upon the king's heart to allow him to go. -

Nehemiah comes to the governors beyond the river and gives them the king's letters, and the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with him, an armed escort to see him safe. When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, hear of it, it grieves them exceedingly that a man has come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel, the same opposition seen when the nation tried to rebuild before. -

Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem and is there three days, then arises in the night with a few men, telling no man what his God had put in his heart to do, for saying too much could ruin the plan. He goes out by night through the gate of the valley, past the dragon well to the dung port, and views the walls of Jerusalem broken down and the gates consumed with fire, then goes on to the gate of the fountain and the king's pool. The rulers do not know where he went or what he did, neither had he yet told the Jews, priests, nobles, rulers, or the rest that did the work.

Nehemiah then tells them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste and its gates are burned; come and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem that we be no more a reproach. He tells them of the good hand of his God upon him and the king's words, and they say, Let us rise up and build, and strengthen their hands for this good work. What is admirable in Nehemiah, as in Ezra, is that he never says the work was of his own knowledge or wisdom, but that the Lord's hand was upon him, and he puts that same vision on the men around him so they strengthen their hands to help.

When Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian hear it, they laugh them to scorn, despise them, and ask what this thing is, and whether they will rebel against the king. Nehemiah answers that the God of heaven will prosper them, and his servants will arise and build, but the mockers have no portion nor right nor memorial in Jerusalem. There was no shame in what he came to do. --- Topics: [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

When Sanballat hears that the wall is being built he is wroth, takes great indignation, and mocks the Jews. One of the heathen rulers rises up against the work, treating the rebuilding of Jerusalem as something to be scorned.

Before his brethren and the army of Samaria, Sanballat mocks the feeble Jews, asking if they will fortify themselves, sacrifice, finish in a day, and revive the burned stones out of the heaps of rubbish. He makes his mockery in front of his army, calling the people weak, the same way the heathen today mock the men who go out in one mind to do the work of the Most High.

Tobiah the Ammonite stands by him and says that even what they build, if a fox go up on it, would break down their stone wall. The enemy despises the work as flimsy, but the builders answer by praying that their reproach be turned upon their own head.

The wall is joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work. This is the pattern for Israel United in Christ today, a people with a mind to work who understand the condition of their people and the mission to rebuild their minds. -
Nehemiah answers the mockery with prayer, asking the Most High to turn the enemies' reproach upon their own heads.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites hear that the walls are going up and the breaches are being stopped, they are very wroth. The breaches are the weaker places the enemies expected would fail. When they hear those gaps are fortified, their anger rises because their expectation of failure is broken.
They conspire together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to hinder the work. Their whole plan is to cause the work to cease and keep the city from being rebuilt. -
The builders make prayer to the Most High and set a watch against the enemies day and night.

Judah says the strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, there is much rubbish, and they are not able to build the wall. Even among the workers the burden grows heavy and discouragement sets in as the enemy pressure mounts.

The adversaries say they will not be known or seen until they come into the midst and slay them and cause the work to cease. The enemies plot a surprise attack, aiming to kill the builders and stop the work entirely.

Nehemiah sets the people in the lower and higher places behind the wall after their families with their swords, spears, and bows. He arms the people by family and posts them at the exposed places, ready to defend the work.

Nehemiah tells the nobles, rulers, and people not to be afraid but to remember the Lord, who is great and terrible, and to fight for their brethren, sons, daughters, wives, and houses. The answer to fear is to remember the greatness of the Most High and to fight for the family and the people.

From that time half of the servants work while the other half hold the spears, shields, and bows, and the rulers stand behind all of Judah. The people labor and guard at the same time, knowing the enemies are plotting against the rebuilding.
Those who bear burdens work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. Every builder keeps a weapon ready even while laying the wall, watchful against attack.

Every builder has his sword girded by his side as he builds, and the one who sounds the trumpet stays by Nehemiah. The trumpet becomes the signal to gather, keeping the scattered workers ready to unite at the point of attack.

Nehemiah tells the people that the work is great and large and they are separated far from one another along the wall. Because the builders are spread out, they need a plan to come together quickly if the enemy strikes.
Wherever they hear the sound of the trumpet, they are to resort there, for the Most High shall fight for them. The confidence of the builders rests on the truth that their God fights for them.
They labor in the work, half of them holding the spears from the rising of the morning until the stars appear. The people work from dawn to nightfall, giving the full day to the task.

Neither Nehemiah, his brethren, his servants, nor the men of the guard put off their clothes, saving only for washing. They are so serious about the work and so watchful that they stay dressed and ready at all times, of one mind to finish the wall, the same way the people are to be of one mind and one spirit today in the resurrection of the people.

When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arabian, and the rest of the enemies hear that the wall is built with no breach left, though the doors are not yet set on the gates, they turn to another plan. With the wall standing, the enemies shift from open threat to schemes against Nehemiah himself.
Sanballat and Geshem send for Nehemiah to meet together in one of the villages in the plain of Ono, but they think to do him mischief. The invitation is a trap to draw Nehemiah away and harm him.

Nehemiah sends messengers saying he is doing a great work and cannot come down, asking why the work should cease while he leaves it to come to them. Nehemiah uses wisdom, refusing to leave the work for a meeting he knows is a plot to put him to death.
They send to him four times after the same manner, and he answers them the same way each time. The enemies keep pressing, and Nehemiah keeps giving the same steady refusal.
The fifth time Sanballat sends his servant with an open letter in his hand. The open letter is meant to be read by others, a public pressure tactic against Nehemiah.

The letter reports among the heathen, and Geshem says it, that Nehemiah and the Jews think to rebel and that this is why he builds the wall, that he may be their king. The enemies invent a charge of rebellion to frighten Nehemiah and give the king cause against him.

The letter claims Nehemiah has appointed prophets to proclaim him king in Judah and threatens to report it to the king, inviting him to take counsel together. The false report is designed to force Nehemiah into their meeting under fear.
Nehemiah answers that there are no such things done as they say, but that they feign them out of their own heart. Nehemiah plainly names the accusation as an invention of their own minds.

They all try to make the builders afraid, saying their hands shall be weakened so the work is not done, and Nehemiah prays for the Most High to strengthen his hands. The whole aim is to weaken the hands and stop the work, so Nehemiah turns to the Most High for strength.

Shemaiah, shut up in his house, tells Nehemiah to meet within the temple and shut the doors because men will come to slay him in the night. A hired man tries to lure Nehemiah into hiding in the temple, framing it as safety.

Nehemiah answers, should such a man as I flee, and who, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life, and says he will not go in. Nehemiah refuses to run or to misuse the temple to save himself, standing firm in his place.

Nehemiah perceives that the Most High had not sent Shemaiah, but that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to pronounce this prophecy. Nehemiah discerns the false prophecy and sees the hand of the enemies who paid for it.

Shemaiah was hired so that Nehemiah would be afraid, do so, and sin, giving them matter for an evil report to reproach him. The scheme is to trap Nehemiah into a fearful sin they could use to shame him.

Nehemiah asks the Most High to think upon Tobiah, Sanballat, the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets who would have put him in fear according to their works. He commits the hired accusers and false prophets to the judgment of the Most High.
The wall is finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. Despite all the plots, the whole wall is completed in fifty-two days.

When the enemies and all the heathen about them hear of it, they are much cast down in their own eyes, for they perceive that the work was wrought of the Most High. The completed wall shames the enemies, who recognize that this was the work and pleasure of the Most High.
In those days the nobles of Judah send many letters to Tobiah, and his letters come to them. Even inside Judah some remain tied to Tobiah, keeping a line of communication with the enemy.

Many in Judah are sworn to Tobiah because he is the son-in-law of Shechaniah and his son married the daughter of Meshullam. Marriage alliances bind some of Judah to the enemy, dividing loyalty within the people.

They report Tobiah's good deeds before Nehemiah and carry Nehemiah's words to Tobiah, and Tobiah sends letters to put him in fear. To the end the enemy uses those inside to pressure and frighten Nehemiah, the same way anything that can be done to stop the work of the Most High is still done today, and the people must keep their spiritual eyes open to see it. --- Topics: [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the offerings of the Lord made by fire, and his inheritance. Therefore shall they have no inheritance among their brethren: the Lord is their inheritance, as he hath said unto them.

This shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether ox or sheep: they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. The firstfruit also of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep, shalt thou give him. For the Most High hath chosen him out of all thy tribes to stand to minister in the name of the Lord, him and his sons for ever.

If a Levite come from any of thy gates out of all Israel, and come with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the Lord shall choose, then he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God, as all his brethren the Levites do which stand there before the Lord. They shall have like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony.

When thou art come into the land, thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations: there shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. These things actually existed and they are all real: wizards, necromancers, divination, observers of times, people that consult with familiar spirits. If they were not real, they would not be in the Bible with the Most High telling us not to do them. All that do these things are an abomination unto the Lord, and because of these abominations the Most High driveth those nations out from before thee. Thou shalt be perfect with the Lord thy God, meaning upright; the nations hearken unto observers of times and unto diviners, but as for thee, the Most High hath not suffered thee so to do.

The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken. This is talking about Christ, Yeshua. This answers what Israel desired of the Most High in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not; and the Lord said, They have well spoken that which they have spoken. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him; and whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him. If we do not follow Christ and do what Christ says, that judgment falls on us.

The prophet which shall presume to speak a word in the name of the Most High which he hath not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die. By this law a lot of these pastors stand condemned: they say things and claim Christ said them, when the Most High never commanded Christ to say it and Christ is not telling them to say it. How shall we know the word which the Lord hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the Lord, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord hath not spoken; the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously, and thou shalt not be afraid of him. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)
